reason: The general sense is rendered consistently as "power", but the countable sense (a miraculous deed, usually plural δυνάμεις) is rendered five ways across chapters: "mighty works" (Matt 7:22; 13:54, 58), "miracles" (Matt 11:20-23; 1 Cor 12:10, 28, 29; Gal 3:5), "deeds of power" (Mark 6:2, 5; 9:39; Luke 10:13; 19:37; Acts 2:22), "works of power" (Acts 8:13; 19:11) and "acts of power" (2 Cor 12:12; Heb 2:4). Even the parallel sayings Matt 11:21 and Luke 10:13 differ.
sense: Countable sense only: a deed that displays supernatural power, a miracle. Usually plural, as something done, worked, seen, or listed beside signs and wonders; singular in Mark 6:5 and 9:39.

alternates.when: The general, non-countable sense: might or capability, of God, Christ, the Spirit, persons or things. Also the plural for forces at work in someone (Matt 14:2; Mark 6:14; Heb 6:5), for heavenly or cosmic powers (Matt 24:29; Mark 13:25; Luke 21:26; Rom 8:38; 1 Cor 15:24; Eph 1:21; 1 Pet 3:22), and, capitalised, as a title for God or a divine being (Matt 26:64; Mark 14:62; Acts 8:10).
A person's or thing's own capacity or resources: Matt 25:15 (ability), 2 Cor 1:8 (strength), 2 Cor 8:3 (means), Rev 1:16 (the sun in its strength). Rev 3:8 may be either "power" or "strength".
The force or sense of a word or language (1 Cor 14:11).
A descriptive genitive that English turns more naturally with an adjective (Heb 1:3 "his powerful word"; optionally 2 Thess 1:7).

traditional: mighty work or miracle (the KJV uses both for this sense)
rationale: The Greek word is simply the ordinary word for power used of a concrete act, and a first-century reader would have heard that connection. "Deed of power" keeps the connection visible where the same word appears nearby as "power" (Mark 6:2 with 6:14; Acts 8:10 with 8:13; 1 Cor 12), which "miracle" hides. It also keeps the word distinct from "sign" and "wonder" in the triads at Acts 2:22, 2 Cor 12:12 and Heb 2:4. It is a standard lexicon gloss and is already the commonest non-traditional choice in the run.
standard_view: There is no dispute about the meaning, only about the English. The KJV alternates "mighty works" and "miracles"; RSV and ESV favour "mighty works" in the Gospels and "miracles" in the letters; NIV and many others use "miracles" throughout; NRSV largely uses "deeds of power". Standard lexica gloss this sense as deed of power, miracle, or wonder. "Miracle" is a fully acceptable rendering, and the default here is a choice for consistency and transparency, not a correction.
